name: Albariño

lines.s10: Albariño is the crisp, dry Atlantic white of north west Spain: white peach, lime and a breath of sea salt.
lines.s20: Albariño comes from Rías Baixas, on the wet, green Atlantic coast of Galicia in north west Spain. It tastes of white peach, lime and grapefruit with a salty finish, bone dry and bright, and it rarely sees oak.
lines.s45: Albariño grows within sight of the Atlantic, in Rías Baixas, on the rainy green coast of north west Spain. It tastes of white peach, apricot and lime, with a salty edge like sea spray. It is dry and light, with high, mouth watering acidity. Most is made in steel tanks and bottled young, with no oak. Across the river Miño, in Portugal, it is called Alvarinho and is often a touch riper and rounder. Pour it with oysters, grilled prawns or octopus. The vines are trained overhead on granite posts, high enough to walk beneath, so the sea wind can dry the grapes after rain.
lines.sale: Albariño gives you ripe peach on the nose and the bite of lime on the tongue, with a salty finish. I would pour it cold with the raw oysters, or with shrimp grilled in garlic and lemon.

glass.lead: White peach, apricot and lime with honeysuckle and a salty, wet stone finish, light, dry and sharply fresh.

ladder.where: Val do Salnés, on the coast of Rías Baixas
O Rosal and Condado do Tea; Monção e Melgaço in Portugal

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity high, alcohol moderate, body light to medium, with a faint, pithy bitterness on the finish and rarely any oak.

home.home: Rías Baixas, on the cool, wet Atlantic coast of Galicia, where the vines stand on granite and are trained overhead on pergolas to keep the bunches dry. A wine labelled Rías Baixas Albariño is the grape alone. It is usually fermented cold in steel and bottled young; some rests on its lees, and a little sees oak.
home.abroad: Across the Miño in Portugal it is Alvarinho, the fuller white of Vinho Verde, above all from Monção e Melgaço. Uruguay's Atlantic coast, California and New Zealand grow it too, in the same crisp, unoaked style.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius: cold, but not so cold that the peach goes quiet.
service.glass: A white wine glass, tapered to hold the perfume.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary; open it cold and pour.
service.age: Drunk young, within one to three years; old vine and lees aged bottles keep a few years longer.

labels.means: The denomination on Galicia's Atlantic coast; labelled Rías Baixas Albariño, the wine is the grape alone.
The grape's Portuguese name, on Vinho Verde from Monção e Melgaço and beyond.
The coolest, most coastal subzone of Rías Baixas, around Cambados: the leanest, saltiest wines.
Warmer subzones on the Miño, where Albariño may be blended with Loureira or Treixadura.
On the lees: the wine was kept on its spent yeast for a rounder texture.

guest.a: No. It smells of ripe peach and apricot, which can suggest sweetness, but it is bone dry, with high acidity and a salty finish.

guest.q: I usually drink Sauvignon Blanc. Will I like this?
guest.a: Very likely. It is as crisp and as dry, but the fruit is peach and lime where Sauvignon Blanc has cut grass, and the finish is salty.

guest.q: The Portuguese list says Alvarinho. Is that the same grape?
guest.a: Yes. Alvarinho is its name across the river in Portugal, where it makes the fuller whites of Vinho Verde, above all in Monção e Melgaço.

compare.tell: Dry Riesling shows lime, green apple and petrol with even sharper acidity; Albariño is peachier, with a salty finish and no petrol.
Pinot Grigio is more neutral and less salty, with pear and a soft finish; Albariño has more perfume, more acidity and a briny edge.
Godello is broader, stonier and quieter on the nose, often with a creamy feel from its lees; Albariño is more scented, lighter and saltier.

cards.front: Albariño: which region is home, on what soil and what training?
cards.back: Rías Baixas, on Galicia's cool, wet Atlantic coast. Granite soils, and vines trained overhead on pergolas, the parra, so that air can dry the bunches after rain.

cards.front: What is Albariño called in Portugal, and where is its home there?
cards.back: Alvarinho. It makes the fuller, still whites of Vinho Verde, above all in the sub-region of Monção e Melgaço, across the Miño from Rías Baixas.

cards.front: Albariño blind: what parts it from a dry Riesling?
cards.back: White peach and apricot with a salty, pithy finish and no petrol. Riesling shows lime and green apple, still sharper acidity and, with age, petrol.

questions.q: A blind white is pale lemon with green tints, dry and unoaked: white peach, apricot and lime, high acidity, moderate alcohol and a salty, faintly bitter finish. Which grape and origin fit it?
questions.exp: Peach and apricot with high acidity, a salty finish and no oak point to Albariño from the Atlantic coast. Viognier shares the apricot but is fuller, with low acidity and more alcohol.

questions.q: A guest orders a bottle labelled Rías Baixas Albariño and asks whether it is a blend. What do you tell her?
questions.exp: A wine labelled Rías Baixas Albariño is made wholly of the grape. The 70 per cent rule belongs to the subzone labels, such as Rosal, which may blend in Loureira.

questions.q: A guest loved the Albariño she drank in Spain and now sees Alvarinho on a Portuguese list. Which region is that bottle most likely to come from?
questions.exp: Alvarinho is the Portuguese name of Albariño, and its home there is Vinho Verde, above all Monção e Melgaço. The Douro's whites rest on other grapes, such as Gouveio and Rabigato.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: Rías Baixas, with Alvarinho in Vinho Verde and the plantings in Uruguay, California and New Zealand given as abroad.
Say opens on the Court's own ahl-bah-REE-nyo and adds the Portuguese Alvarinho.

No Codex record is contradicted. The profile, the dials, the grid read for Rías Baixas and the region records for Rías Baixas and Vinho Verde supplied the fruit, the structure, the pergola, the granite, the label rule of the grape alone and the 70 per cent subzone labels.

The ladder has two rungs: Val do Salnés as the cool coast, and O Rosal, Condado do Tea and Monção e Melgaço as the warmer, more inland ground, which is how the Codex's region records and the denomination's own pages read them.
Alvarinho as a touch riper and rounder is hedged with often: Monção e Melgaço is warmer and drier than the coast of Rías Baixas, and the Codex calls its wine the fuller white of Vinho Verde.

California stands on the plan's own note and on The Oxford Companion to Wine; the Codex's region records name Uruguay, Marlborough, Nelson, Long Island and Virginia for the grape. The year the grape reached Uruguay was left out: the one page that gives it carries a living writer's name in its title.
The Gulf oysters are the one dish from the Creole table.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
